summary: The second-generation iX3 is the first Neue Klasse BMW, built on a dedicated 800V platform with a Gen6 cylindrical-cell battery, and Australian reviewers have been close to unanimous that it is the new benchmark premium electric SUV — steering, braking feel and regeneration are singled out as the best of any EV they have driven. Its range claim is among the longest of any new vehicle on sale in Australia — 788km WLTP for the M Sport-equipped car on 20-inch wheels that Australia gets, against the 805km headline BMW quotes for a European base car — and at $112,500 before on-roads (up $2,600 from its $109,900 launch price) it still undercuts the Porsche Macan, Audi Q6 e-tron quattro and Polestar 3 rather than matching them. The disagreement is over the tech-first cabin: the 43-inch Panoramic Vision strip impresses everyone, but reviewers split on whether burying climate and steering-wheel adjustment in a screen-heavy iDrive is livable, and several flagged rear-seat harshness on passive dampers as an open question for Australian roads.
pros: 788km WLTP for the M Sport-spec 50 xDrive on 20-inch wheels is among the longest ranges of any new vehicle on sale in Australia — Polestar 3 claims 706km and the Audi Q6 e-tron 542km
800V architecture charges at up to 400kW, adding a claimed 372km in 10 minutes and 10-80 per cent in about 21 minutes
Undercuts the premium electric SUVs it is benchmarked against by thousands: rivals from Porsche, Audi and Polestar sit in the $120,000-$140,000 band
345kW/645Nm dual-motor drivetrain does 0-100km/h in 4.9 seconds, and reviewers rate the steering feel and near-98-per-cent regenerative braking as the best in any EV they have driven
2000kg braked tow rating and a 520L boot plus a 58L frunk — the first BMW EV with front storage
cons: Only one grade is confirmed orderable: the 50 xDrive, which BMW raised $2,600 to $112,500 four months after launch. The $89,900 rear-drive iX3 40, which would sit under the $91,661 luxury car tax threshold, is priced but its Q4 2026 deliveries were still unconfirmed in late November 2026
Air-conditioning and even steering-wheel adjustment are screen-only, and reviewers called the Panoramic iDrive laggy, illogically nested and steep enough to need a lengthy instructional briefing
Rear-seat ride was described as harsh over sharp inputs, and there is no driver-adjustable damper option — a live risk on Australian roads given launch cars were assessed on smooth Spanish tarmac
No spare tyre of any kind, only run-flats; one launch car was stranded by a puncture

Real-world consumption of 17.3-18kWh/100km in testing implies roughly 600-650km rather than the near-800km lab claim, the optional 22-inch wheels cut the WLTP figure to 737km, and BMW's five-year warranty trails the seven years Kia offers on the EV9
